claims.claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of 3×HATom1 or 3×HATom1CA with Rpl26aFLAG was only detected in low MW fractions.
claims.source: Co-immunoprecipitation of 3×HATom1 or 3×HATom1CA with Rpl26aFLAG was only detected in these low MW fractions (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from fractionated samples shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG detected in low MW fractions from bortezomib-treated cells was almost entirely lost from tom1CA cells.
claims.source: Moreover, ubiquitinated Rpl26aFLAG detected in low MW fractions from bortezomib-treated cells was almost entirely lost from tom1CA cells (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by UBA pull-down data from fractionated samples shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Tom1 localizes to the nucleus and nucleolus.
claims.source: Consistent with the reported localization of Tom1 (Huh et al., 2003), Rpl26aFLAG or Rpl26aGFP that accumulated upon their transient overexpression in tom1CA cells were found in the nucleus and nucleolus (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is consistent with the localization data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Rpl26aFLAG or Rpl26aGFP that accumulated upon their transient overexpression in tom1CA cells were found in the nucleus and nucleolus.
claims.source: Consistent with the reported localization of Tom1 (Huh et al., 2003), Rpl26aFLAG or Rpl26aGFP that accumulated upon their transient overexpression in tom1CA cells were found in the nucleus and nucleolus (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Overexpressed Rpl26a failed to assemble into ribosomes and was directly bound and ubiquitinated by Tom1 in the nuclear/nucleolar compartments.
claims.source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that overexpressed Rpl26a failed to assemble into ribosomes and was directly bound and ubiquitinated by Tom1 in the nuclear/nucleolar compartments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from fractionation, co-immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination, and localization experiments.

claims.claim: Deletion of TOM1 enabled increased accumulation of at least seven of eight ectopically overexpressed ribosomal proteins.
claims.source: Similar to what we observed with bortezomib (Sung et al., 2016), deletion of TOM1 enabled increased accumulation of at least seven of them (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry of 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates from bortezomib-treated cells revealed enrichment for several ribosomal proteins, including Rpl26b.
claims.source: Mass spectrometry of 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates from bortezomib-treated cells revealed enrichment for several ribosomal proteins, including Rpl26b (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Ribosomal proteins are commonly identified in purified ubiquitin conjugates.
claims.source: Ribosomal proteins are commonly identified in purified ubiquitin conjugates (Mayor et al., 2007, 2005; Peng et al., 2003) or in ubiquitination site mapping experiments that rely on purification of the GlyGly dipeptide that remains attached to a lysine side chain following digestion of an ubiquitin conjugate with trypsin (Kim et al., 2011; Lesmantavicius et al., 2014; Porras-Yakushi and Hess, 2014; Porras-Yakushi et al., 2015; Sarraf et al., 2013; Swaney et al., 2013; Udeshi et al., 2013b; Wagner et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: GlyGly profiling of tom1∆ and TOM1 cells revealed 1980 unique ubiquitination sites in 920 distinct proteins, of which 972 unique sites in 532 proteins were quantified.
claims.source: Analysis of three biological replicates (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 3B) revealed 1980 unique ubiquitination sites in 920 distinct proteins, of which 972 unique sites in 532 proteins were quantified.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from GlyGly profiling experiments.

claims.claim: All three tom1∆ biological replicates exhibited lower overall ubiquitination than wild type.
claims.source: All three tom1∆ biological replicates exhibited lower overall ubiquitination than wild type, suggesting a major role for Tom1 in PQC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of GlyGly profiling data.

claims.claim: Of the 141 ubiquitination sites that exhibited a ≥two-fold decrease in ubiquitination in tom1∆, 51 (36%) were in ribosomal proteins.
claims.source: Of the 141 sites that exhibited a ≥two-fold decrease in ubiquitination in tom1∆, 51 (36%) were in ribosomal proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GlyGly profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Of the ubiquitinated peptides derived from ribosomal proteins, >50% (51 of 101) decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
claims.source: Moreover, of the ubiquitinated peptides derived from ribosomal proteins, >50% (51 of 101) decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GlyGly profiling data.

claims.claim: Of 837 non-ribosomal ubiquitination sites identified, only 11% decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
claims.source: By comparison, of 837 non-ribosomal sites identified, only 11% decreased in abundance in tom1∆.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of GlyGly profiling data.

claims.claim: The reduction in ribosomal ubiquitin conjugates in tom1∆ was not due to reduction in total ribosomal protein levels.
claims.source: SILAC analysis of the unfractionated cell lysates indicated that the reduction in ribosomal ubiquitin conjugates in tom1∆ was not due to reduction in total ribosomal protein levels (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by SILAC analysis of total protein levels shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Gene ontology analysis of the GlyGly profiling data confirmed that ubiquitination of ribosomal proteins, particularly those of the large (60S) subunit, was disproportionately impacted by loss of Tom1.
claims.source: Gene ontology analysis of the GlyGly profiling data confirmed that ubiquitination of ribosomal proteins (Figure 3C), particularly those of the large (60S) subunit (Figure 3D), was disproportionately impacted by loss of Tom1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of GlyGly profiling data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claims.claim: The strong effects on ribosomal protein ubiquitination seen in tom1∆ cells were due specifically to loss of Tom1's E3 activity.
claims.source: To address whether the strong effects on ribosomal protein ubiquitination seen in tom1∆ cells were due specifically to loss of Tom1's E3 activity, the GlyGly SILAC analysis was repeated with WT and tom1CA cells. Quantitative analysis of the data confirmed a disproportionate loss of ribosomal protein ubiquitination (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GlyGly profiling data comparing WT and tom1CA cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Detergent-insoluble proteins, including Rpl1 and Rpl3, were greatly increased in tom1∆ cells compared to WT cells.
claims.source: Detergent-insoluble proteins, including Rpl1 and Rpl3, were greatly increased in tom1∆ cells compared to WT cells (Figure 3F, Pellet).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining and Western blot analysis of detergent-insoluble fractions shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: High accumulation of insoluble proteins in tom1∆ cells was evident regardless of the method or buffer employed for cell lysis.
claims.source: High accumulation of insoluble proteins in tom1∆ cells was evident regardless of the method or buffer employed for cell lysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A testing different lysis conditions.

claims.claim: The insoluble proteins that exhibited the largest increase in tom1∆ cells were ribosomal proteins including Rpl1 and Rpl3.
claims.source: The insoluble proteins that exhibited the largest increase in tom1∆ cells were ribosomal proteins including Rpl1 and Rpl3 (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, and Supplementary file 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Ribosomal proteins, including those of both the 60S and 40S subunits, comprise the major class of aggregating proteins in tom1∆ cells.
claims.source: Gene ontology analysis (Figure 3H) and a plot of the top 20 detergent-insoluble proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C) indicated that ribosomal proteins, including those of both the 60S and 40S subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D) comprise the major class of aggregating proteins in tom1∆ cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3H and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Two positively-charged clusters in Rpl26 – RRKARK (amino acids 12–17) and a patch formed by R27, R28, R51, and R52 – mediate binding to 5.8S rRNA and assembly into ribosomes.
claims.source: Two positively-charged clusters in Rpl26 – RRKARK (amino acids 12–17) and a patch formed by R27, R28, R51, and R52 – mediate binding to 5.8S rRNA and assembly into ribosomes (Babiano et al., 2012) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is illustrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Some mutants of Rpl26a with mutations in rRNA-binding residues exhibited even less accumulation than overexpressed WT Rpl26aFLAG.
claims.source: We mutated various combinations of these residues to glutamate and observed that some mutants exhibited even less accumulation than overexpressed WT Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Rpl26-4EFLAG (R12E, R13E, R16E, K17E) did not accumulate or assemble into ribosomes in rpl26a∆rpl26b∆ cells.
claims.source: Unlike WT Rpl26aFLAG, Rpl26-4EFLAG(R12E, R13E, R16E, K17E) did not accumulate or assemble into ribosomes in rpl26a∆rpl26b∆ cells (Figure 4C, top panels).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Upon inhibition of the proteasome with MG132 or bortezomib, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated and was detected in the low MW fractions of a sucrose gradient.
claims.source: However, upon inhibition of the proteasome with MG132 or bortezomib, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was detected in the low MW fractions of a sucrose gradient (Figure 4C, bottom panels), where it was ubiquitinated, albeit to a lesser extent than unassembled WT Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose gradient fractionation data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary data.

claims.claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG was ubiquitinated to a lesser extent than unassembled WT Rpl26aFLAG.
claims.source: However, upon inhibition of the proteasome with MG132 or bortezomib, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was detected in the low MW fractions of a sucrose gradient (Figure 4C, bottom panels), where it was ubiquitinated, albeit to a lesser extent than unassembled WT Rpl26aFLAG (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by UBA pull-down data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1.
claims.source: Strikingly, Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1 (Figure 4E) and showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆ (Figure 4F), suggesting that it is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆.
claims.source: Strikingly, Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1 (Figure 4E) and showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆ (Figure 4F), suggesting that it is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
claims.source: Strikingly, Rpl26a-4EFLAG exhibited poor association with 3xHATom1 (Figure 4E) and showed only very weak accumulation in tom1∆ (Figure 4F), suggesting that it is not primarily a Tom1 substrate but is re-directed to another QC pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the poor association with Tom1 and weak accumulation in tom1∆ cells.

claims.claim: Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated in doa10 mutants.
claims.source: Consistent with this idea, Rpl26a-4EFLAG accumulated in doa10 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The failure of Rpl26a-4EFLAG to be targeted by Tom1 was not due to a defect in its nuclear localization.
claims.source: The failure of Rpl26a-4EFLAG to be targeted by Tom1 was not due to a defect in its nuclear localization (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Residues of Rpl26a that mediate interactions with rRNA and are buried when incorporated into the ribosome are required for ubiquitination by Tom1 when Rpl26a fails to assemble.
claims.source: Taken together, our results suggest that residues of Rpl26a that mediate interactions with rRNA and are buried when incorporated into the ribosome are also required for ubiquitination by Tom1 when Rpl26a fails to assemble.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined mutagenesis and ubiquitination data for Rpl26a.

claims.claim: Upon its synthesis, Rpl4 binds the dedicated chaperone Acl4.
claims.source: Upon its synthesis, Rpl4 binds the dedicated chaperone Acl4. The Rpl4–Acl4 then recruits the karyopherin Kap104, for import into the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Rpl4 assembly.

claims.claim: The Rpl4–Acl4 complex recruits the karyopherin Kap104 for import into the nucleus.
claims.source: Upon its synthesis, Rpl4 binds the dedicated chaperone Acl4. The Rpl4–Acl4 then recruits the karyopherin Kap104, for import into the nucleus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on Rpl4 assembly.

claims.claim: K55 and K308 of Rpl4, whose ubiquitinations exhibited the strongest dependence on Tom1, contact rRNA and are not accessible for modification in the mature ribosome.
claims.source: The crystal structure of the ribosome indicates that K55 and K308, whose ubiquitinations exhibited the strongest dependence on Tom1, contact rRNA and are not accessible for modification in the mature ribosome (Ben-Shem et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the ribosome crystal structure and GlyGly profiling data.

claims.claim: The crystal structure of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex revealed that Acl4 conceals K55.
claims.source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex revealed that Acl4 conceals K55, and a structural model of Kap104 docked to Acl4–Rpl4 indicates that it protects K308 and K338.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex.

claims.claim: A structural model of Kap104 docked to Acl4–Rpl4 indicates that it protects K308 and K338.
claims.source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of the Acl4–Rpl4 complex revealed that Acl4 conceals K55, and a structural model of Kap104 docked to Acl4–Rpl4 indicates that it protects K308 and K338.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling of the Acl4–Rpl4–Kap104 complex.

claims.claim: Upon import of Rpl4–Acl4–Kap104 into the nucleus, Kap104 is dissociated through the action of Ran-GTP.
claims.source: Upon import of Rpl4–Acl4–Kap104 into the nucleus, Kap104 is dissociated through the action of Ran-GTP (Kressler et al., 2012)(F. H. and A. H., submitted).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates readily ubiquitinated Rpl4 in binary Acl4–Rpl4 complexes but not in ternary Acl4–Rpl4–ctKap104 complexes.
claims.source: 3xHATom1 immunoprecipitates readily ubiquitinated Rpl4 in binary Acl4–Rpl4 complexes but not in ternary Acl4–Rpl4–ctKap104 complexes, despite the fact that at least eight lysines of Rpl4 should remain exposed in the ternary complex (red circle, Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Ubiquitination of Rpl4 within the binary Acl4–Rpl4 complex required its extended C-terminus because it was eliminated when the C-terminal region was truncated at residue 276.
claims.source: Ubiquitination of Rpl4 within the binary complex required its extended C-terminus because it was eliminated when the C-terminal region was truncated at residue 276 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data with truncated Rpl4 shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Tom1 selectively recognizes and ubiquitinates ribosomal proteins via residues that are only accessible in the unassembled state.
claims.source: These data, along with those on Rpl26a, suggest that Tom1 selectively recognizes and ubiquitinates ribosomal proteins via residues that are only accessible in the unassembled state.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Rpl26a and Rpl4 experiments.

claims.claim: Of the 18 lysines from large subunit ribosomal proteins that could be observed in the 4V88 structure, 13 in the free 60S and 15 in the assembled 80S were not accessible to the probe.
claims.source: Of the 18 lysines that could be observed in the 4V88 structure, 13 in the free 60S and 15 in the assembled 80S were not accessible to the probe (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Tom1-dependent ubiquitination events generally occur on ribosomal proteins prior to their assembly into the ribosome, on residues that normally are either buried in the ribosome, engage in salt bridges, or are otherwise shielded from contact.
claims.source: Taken together, our data suggest strongly that Tom1-dependent ubiquitination events generally occur on ribosomal proteins prior to their assembly into the ribosome, on residues that normally are either buried in the ribosome, engage in salt bridges, or are otherwise shielded from contact.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined structural and experimental data.

claims.claim: tom1CA cells were extremely sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A from the GAL10 promoter.
claims.source: First, tom1CA cells (but not WT cells) were extremely sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A (Figure 6A) but not RPL26A-4E (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) from the GAL10 promoter.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: tom1CA cells were not sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A-4E from the GAL10 promoter.
claims.source: First, tom1CA cells (but not WT cells) were extremely sensitive to constitutive overexpression of RPL26A (Figure 6A) but not RPL26A-4E (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) from the GAL10 promoter.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Depletion of Rrn3, Rpa190, or Hmo1 caused a synthetic growth defect when combined with tom1CA.
claims.source: Second, we created a situation in which ribosomal proteins as a group are made in excess of rRNA via depletion (using the auxin-inducible degron (AID) [Morawska and Ulrich, 2013]) of proteins involved in rRNA synthesis including Rrn3 (transcription factor for RNA polymerase I), Rpa190 (RNA polymerase I largest subunit) and Hmo1 (regulator of transcription by RNA polymerase I). claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The effect of combining hmo1∆ and tom1CA mutations was even more severe than depletion of Rrn3 or Rpa190 combined with tom1CA.
claims.source: The effect of combining hmo1∆ and tom1CA mutations was even more severe (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Inactivation of TOM1 in an acl4∆ background caused a substantial synthetic growth defect.
claims.source: Third, we manipulated cells such that assembly of a single ribosomal protein was impaired, via deletion of the Rpl4-selective chaperone Acl4 (Stelter et al., 2015). Inactivation of TOM1 in an acl4∆ background caused a substantial synthetic growth defect (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: There was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when RNA Pol I transcription was diminished (hmo1∆tom1CA) in a tom1CA background.
claims.source: Strikingly, there was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when RNA Pol I transcription was diminished (hmo1∆tom1CA; Figure 6D) or Rpl4 assembly was perturbed (acl4∆tom1CA; Figure 6E) in a tom1CA background.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: There was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when Rpl4 assembly was perturbed (acl4∆tom1CA) in a tom1CA background.
claims.source: Strikingly, there was a massive increase in detergent-insoluble proteins when RNA Pol I transcription was diminished (hmo1∆tom1CA; Figure 6D) or Rpl4 assembly was perturbed (acl4∆tom1CA; Figure 6E) in a tom1CA background.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Deletions in 36 different genes encoding ribosomal proteins exhibit synthetic negative genetic interaction with tom1∆.
claims.source: In addition to suppressors that map to stress response/chaperone pathways and genes involved in ribosome protein expression (PKA pathway), deletions in 36 different genes encoding ribosomal proteins exhibit synthetic negative genetic interaction with tom1∆ (Costanzo et al., 2010) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is summarized in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to a synthetic growth defect in a tom1∆ mutant.
claims.source: Consistent with this prediction, deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to a synthetic growth defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in a tom1∆ mutant (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in a tom1∆ mutant.
claims.source: Consistent with this prediction, deletion of one of the two copies of RPS29 led to a synthetic growth defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) and enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in a tom1∆ mutant (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Coomassie staining of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 6F.

results.result: Tom1 E3 ubiquitin ligase and E2 enzymes Ubc4/Ubc5 mediate ubiquitination and degradation of overexpressed Rpl26a that fails to assemble into ribosomes in the nucleus/nucleolus.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary experimental approaches (Western blots, co-IP, in vitro ubiquitination assays, sucrose gradient fractionation, subcellular localization) consistently demonstrate that Tom1 and Ubc4/Ubc5 are required for ubiquitination of unassembled Rpl26a in the nuclear/nucleolar compartment. The data show accumulation in mutants (C16, C21), loss of ubiquitination (C18, C22, C28), direct binding (C23), and in vitro activity (C24, C25), providing strong converging evidence.

results.result: Tom1 broadly mediates ubiquitination of multiple ribosomal proteins, with >50% of ribosomal protein ubiquitination sites showing Tom1-dependence, particularly affecting large (60S) subunit proteins.
results.evaluation: GlyGly profiling with SILAC quantification across three biological replicates provides robust proteome-wide evidence (C35-C39). The data show that 51 of 101 (>50%) ribosomal protein ubiquitination sites decreased in tom1Δ, while only 11% of non-ribosomal sites were affected (C38-C39). Gene ontology analysis and comparison with tom1CA mutants confirm specificity (C41-C42). Total protein levels were unchanged, ruling out indirect effects (C40).

results.result: tom1 mutants accumulate high levels of detergent-insoluble ribosomal proteins, with ribosomal proteins comprising the major class of aggregating proteins.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent approaches (Coomassie staining, Western blots, mass spectrometry with iBAQ quantification, gene ontology analysis) consistently demonstrate massive accumulation of insoluble ribosomal proteins in tom1Δ cells (C43-C46). The phenotype is robust across different lysis methods and buffers (C44), and mass spectrometry identifies ribosomal proteins as the predominant class of insoluble proteins (C45-C46).

results.result: Tom1 recognizes and ubiquitinates ribosomal proteins via residues that mediate rRNA binding and are buried in mature ribosomes, as demonstrated by mutagenesis of Rpl26a rRNA-binding residues.
results.evaluation: Systematic mutagenesis of Rpl26a rRNA-binding residues (C47-C48) shows that the 4E mutant (R12E, R13E, R16E, K17E) fails to accumulate in tom1Δ (C53), exhibits poor Tom1 binding (C52), shows reduced ubiquitination (C51), and is redirected to Doa10 pathway (C54-C55). The mutant retains nuclear localization (C56), ruling out mislocalization as explanation. These data provide strong mechanistic insight into substrate recognition.

results.result: Tom1 selectively ubiquitinates Rpl4 in the binary Acl4-Rpl4 complex but not in the ternary Acl4-Rpl4-Kap104 complex, targeting residues that contact rRNA and are inaccessible in mature ribosomes.
results.evaluation: In vitro ubiquitination assays with purified components demonstrate that Tom1 ubiquitinates Rpl4 in binary but not ternary complexes (C64), requiring the C-terminal region (C65). GlyGly profiling identifies K55 and K308 as major Tom1-dependent sites (C60), and structural analysis shows these residues contact rRNA in mature ribosomes (C60) and are protected by chaperones/karyopherins in assembly intermediates (C61-C62). This provides independent validation of the substrate recognition mechanism.

results.result: Structural analysis reveals that 83% (15 of 18) of major Tom1-dependent ubiquitination sites on large subunit ribosomal proteins are inaccessible in the mature 80S ribosome.
results.evaluation: Systematic mapping of Tom1-dependent ubiquitination sites onto the ribosome structure (PDB 4V88) using a HECT domain-ubiquitin complex probe shows that 15 of 18 sites are not accessible in assembled ribosomes (C67, C93). This structural analysis provides independent validation of the biochemical findings and supports the model that Tom1 targets unassembled forms (C68, C92).

results.result: tom1CA mutants exhibit hypersensitivity to imbalances in ribosome component production, including overexpression of RPL26A, depletion of rRNA synthesis factors, loss of Rpl4 chaperone Acl4, and reduction of single ribosomal protein expression.
results.evaluation: Multiple independent genetic perturbations that create ribosome component imbalances all cause synthetic growth defects with tom1CA (C69, C71-C73, C105-C108). The specificity is demonstrated by lack of sensitivity to RPL26A-4E overexpression (C70). Growth defects correlate with massive accumulation of insoluble proteins (C74-C75), suggesting proteostasis collapse. The consistency across diverse perturbations strongly supports a general role in managing ribosome component imbalances.

results.result: Deletion of one copy of duplicated ribosomal protein gene RPS29 causes synthetic growth defects and enormous accumulation of insoluble proteins in tom1Δ mutants, consistent with genetic interaction data showing 36 ribosomal protein genes exhibit synthetic negative interactions with tom1Δ.
results.evaluation: The RPS29 deletion experiment (C77-C78) provides direct validation of predictions from genome-wide genetic interaction data (C76). Both growth defects and massive protein aggregation are observed, consistent with the broader pattern of genetic interactions. This validates the physiological relevance of the ERISQ pathway under conditions of ribosome component imbalance.

results.result: tom1Δ cells accumulate significantly more insoluble proteins than other major PQC pathway mutants (doa10Δ, hrd1Δ, ltn1Δ, san1Δ, ubr1Δ), establishing ERISQ as a major proteostasis pathway.
results.evaluation: Direct comparison of insoluble protein accumulation across multiple well-characterized PQC mutants shows tom1Δ has the highest burden (C79, C111). This quantitative comparison provides strong evidence for the physiological importance of ERISQ relative to other known PQC pathways (C80). The comparison is fair as all mutants were analyzed under identical conditions.

results.result: The ERISQ pathway is conserved in human cells, where Huwe1 (Tom1 homolog) mediates ubiquitination and degradation of overexpressed hRpl26, with prior GlyGly profiling showing Huwe1-dependent ubiquitination of multiple ribosomal proteins.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary approaches in human cells demonstrate conservation: proteasome inhibitors enable hRpl26 accumulation (C82), Huwe1 knockdown/knockout enables accumulation (C83-C84), overexpressed hRpl26 is stable in HUWE1 KO cells (C85), and ubiquitination requires Huwe1 (C86). Prior proteome-wide data show 6 of top 10 Huwe1-dependent ubiquitination sites are on ribosomal proteins (C87, C100). The convergence of current and prior data strongly supports conservation.

results.result: The authors propose that ERISQ (Excess Ribosomal protein Quality control) mediated by Tom1/Ubc4/Ubc5 is a key element of the quality control machinery sustaining protein homeostasis and cellular fitness in eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: This integrative conclusion (C7, C91, C112) is well-supported by the totality of experimental evidence showing: (1) Tom1 broadly targets multiple ribosomal proteins, (2) tom1 mutants accumulate more insoluble proteins than other PQC mutants, (3) tom1 mutants are hypersensitive to ribosome component imbalances, and (4) the pathway is conserved in humans. While the term 'ERISQ' is newly coined, the underlying biology is well-documented.

results.result: The authors propose a kinetic competition model where Tom1 and rRNA compete for binding to ribosomal proteins in the nucleolus, with Tom1 potentially using negatively-charged regions to interact electrostatically with basic ribosomal proteins.
results.evaluation: These are speculative mechanistic models (C94, C97) proposed to explain substrate recognition but not directly tested. While consistent with the data (ribosomal proteins are basic, Tom1 is acidic, ubiquitination sites overlap with rRNA-binding sites), no kinetic measurements or direct tests of electrostatic interactions are provided. The models are reasonable hypotheses requiring future validation.

results.result: tom1 mutants exhibit multiple phenotypes including cell cycle arrest, nucleolar fragmentation, defective mRNA export, reduced transcription, reduced polysomes, and altered rRNA processing, with ERISQ defects observed at permissive temperatures while other defects require heat stress.
results.evaluation: The phenotypic characterization (C101-C102) is supported by citations to prior literature and new data. The temperature-dependence analysis (C103) provides important evidence that ERISQ is a primary defect rather than secondary consequence. The genetic suppression by PKA pathway mutations (C104) adds complexity but is experimentally documented. However, the relationships between these phenotypes remain incompletely resolved.

results.result: Combining tom1 mutations with mutations causing ribosome production imbalances (e.g., tom1CA acl4Δ) leads to enormous increases in insoluble protein, suggesting proteostasis collapse.
results.evaluation: The double mutant analysis (C110) is well-supported by Coomassie staining data showing massive accumulation of insoluble proteins. This provides strong evidence for synthetic proteostasis defects. However, the claim of 'collapse' is somewhat interpretive - while the accumulation is dramatic, cells remain viable enough for analysis.

results.result: The authors propose that unassembled ribosomal proteins may titrate Huwe1 in human cells, potentially creating feedback loops analogous to the Mdm2-p53 pathway that responds to ribosome assembly stress.
results.evaluation: These are speculative hypotheses (C113-C115, C121, C125) connecting ERISQ to known stress response pathways. While the Mdm2-p53 pathway is well-established (C113-C115), the proposed Huwe1 titration mechanism (C125) is not tested. The logic is reasonable given increased ribosome production in cancer (C121), but direct experimental evidence is lacking.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on protein quality control, ribosome biogenesis, ribosomal protein degradation, Tom1 substrates, and connections to human disease and cancer.
results.evaluation: These background claims (C8-C15, C34, C88-C90, C95-C96, C98, C116-C124) are well-supported by citations to prior literature. They establish the context and significance of the work but do not represent new findings from this study. The citations appear appropriate and the general knowledge claims are accurate.
